boundary_note: Bounded first pass for Bodart's battle at Auerstädt on 14 October 1806 in cohort v1's fourth-coalition 1806 group: the 13th and the night of 13-14 October on both sides, Marshal Davout's debouch at Kösen, the meeting at Hassenhausen, the successive Prussian attacks, the flank fight at Sulza, the French advance to Eckartsberga, the Prussian retreat and the losses. Napoleon's battle at Jena the same day is a separate entry (B372a), as are Saalfeld (B371b) and the capitulation of Erfurt (B373b); the 5th Bulletin's results and French loss cover both fields of the 14th. Side A is the French. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.value: Bodart gives side A (French) under Marshal Davout 36 battalions with 26,000 infantry, 9 squadrons with 1,300 cavalry and 44 guns, 27,300 men in all, and side B (Prussians) under General Field Marshal the Duke of Brunswick, whose name he marks with a dagger and whom he lists among the fallen generals (claim bodart-commanders), 52 battalions with 41,000 infantry, 80 squadrons with 9,000 cavalry and 230 guns, 50,000 men in all. By his stated rule his strengths are the forces available for the battle, rounded up.
claims.rationale: Bodart's printed table, read from the page image in the frame transcription; one claim among several. His side A's 26,000 infantry equal the 26,000 combatants that Foucart's note puts present at the battle in all, and his 44 guns the 44 pieces of the 3rd corps's journal (claim foucart-side-a); his 36 battalions are 10 more than the 26 of Foucart's other note, and his 27,300 in all is 1,300 more than Foucart's 26,000 (our arithmetic). His side B's 50,000 equals the 5th Bulletin's corps of 50,000 and the main army of 50,000 in Lieutenant-Colonel von der Goltz's account (claim foucart-side-b) and the 50,000 with which Höpfner has the Prussians march on the 13th (claim hoepfner-side-b); his 52 battalions equal the later Bulletin's 11, 11 and 10 battalions of the King's three divisions and 20 of Kalkreuth's reserve, 52, and his 80 squadrons lie between its 70 and 90, as the reserve's 20 squadrons are read as its total or as each division's (all our arithmetic; claim foucart-side-b). Both armies were on the march when they met, and these are the forces present at the start, so the claim is inherited; how much of side B came into action is claim side-b-engaged. English rendering (ours) of Bodart's rules: p. 46, 'the strengths given are always those forces that were disposable for the battle'; p. 47, 'the strength and loss figures were rounded up by the author'. English rendering (ours) of the entry: '1806 14 October: battle at Auerstädt (2.)'; 'French | Prussians'; 'Marshal Davoust | General Field Marshal Duke of Brunswick †'; '36 battalions 26,000 | infantry | 41,000 battalions 52'; '9 squadrons 1,300 | cavalry | 9,000 squadrons 80'; '44 guns 27,300 | total strength | 50,000 guns 230'. 'Btln.' is Bataillon, 'Esk.' Eskadron, 'Gesch.' Geschütze, 'GFM.' General-Feldmarschall and 'Hz.' Herzog in Bodart's list of abbreviations.

claims.value: Side A in Foucart: by his note the 3rd corps, which counted 28,874 men on its effective strength on 5 October, had on the 14th no more than 26,000 combatants present at the battle, and by another note Marshal Davout had 26 battalions and the corps's line of battle was then 4,000 to 4,500 metres long. In the 3rd corps's journal all the corps's artillery, reserve included, consisted of only 44 pieces of different calibres; from half past 6 to 9 o'clock the division Gudin alone bore the enemy's effort, from 9 to half past 10 the light cavalry and the divisions Gudin and Friant fought together, and from half past 10 to the end of the battle the whole corps was united. Davout reported that the little cavalry he had, though it served very well, was not enough to profit from the infantry's successes, and that the grand-duc de Berg had withdrawn the dragoon division Sahuc the day before. Colonel Blein, quoted by Foucart, heard from an officer taken and brought to the King of Prussia that the King, told that the corps was only 25,000 to 26,000 men, exclaimed that there were certainly more than 50,000.
claims.rationale: Foucart's notes (pp. 678 and 684), the journal (pp. 673 and 683), Davout's report (p. 672) and Blein (p. 682), read from the page images. Foucart's 26,000 present are about 90% of the 28,874 effective (our arithmetic); they equal Bodart's 26,000 infantry, and the journal's 44 pieces Bodart's 44 guns (claim bodart-strength), but Foucart's 26 battalions are 10 fewer than Bodart's 36 (our arithmetic). The journal's hours show the corps coming up by divisions, Gudin's alone until 9 and the whole corps only from half past 10 (claim davout-decision for the march). Blein's figure is what a captured French officer told the King. Which French troops were present followed from Napoleon's orders, the grand-duc de Berg's withdrawal of the dragoons and Bernadotte's march to Dornburg (claim hoepfner-side-a); the passages read do not show Davout concentrating any further force for the battle, so the claim is inherited. English renderings (ours): Foucart's note, '2. The 3rd corps, which counted 28,874 men on the effective strength on 5 October, had not, on the 14th, more than 26,000 combatants present at the battle' (p. 684); '2. The line of battle of the 3rd corps was then 4,000 to 4,500 metres long. Marshal Davout had 26 battalions' (p. 678); the journal, 'extract of the journal of operations of the 3rd army corps' (p. 673); 'from half past 6 to 9 o'clock the division Gudin alone sustained the enemy's effort; from 9 o'clock to half past 10 the light cavalry and the divisions Gudin and Friant fought together; from half past 10 to the end of the battle the whole army corps was united'; 'all the artillery of the 3rd corps, reserve included, consisted of only 44 pieces of different calibres' (p. 683); Davout's report, 'Battle of Auerstädt'; 'Marshal Davout to the Emperor'; 'at the bivouac of Auerstädt, 14 October 1806' (p. 672); 'the number of prisoners is not very considerable, the little cavalry I had, which served very well besides, not having been sufficient to be able to profit from the successes of the infantry'; 'the grand-duc de Berg had withdrawn the dragoon division Sahuc the day before' (p. 672); Blein, '1. « ..... I heard, says Colonel Blein, an officer who had been taken and brought to the King of Prussia relate that this prince, having enquired about the strength of this army corps, when he was told that it was only 25,000 to 26,000 men, exclaimed: « That is a real French boast; there are certainly more than 50,000 men there and you are not showing everything. »' (p. 682).

claims.value: Side A in Höpfner: Napoleon's preliminary orders had already led the grand-duc de Berg to march off up the Saale and take away the dragoon division Sahuc ('Sachuc' in the print). Marshal Davout proposed to Marshal Bernadotte that he debouch behind him as far as Kösen and take command of the united corps of about 56,000 men; Bernadotte understood the order differently and believed he must march to Dornburg, so Davout was left to his own forces, about 33000 men. Davout's divisions reached the field one after another: Gudin's arrived near Hassenhausen at about the same time as the Prussian division Schmettau, Friant's battalions came up gradually and Davout led them as they arrived, and Morand's battalions came up at a full run to reinforce and extend his left; Höpfner's number and strength for Morand's fresh battalions are read only in the OCR (OCR from 'Davout's divisions').
claims.rationale: Höpfner's page image (p. 365) and his narrative from the OCR. His about 33000 is 7,000 more than Foucart's 26,000 present and 5,700 more than Bodart's 27,300 (our arithmetic; claims foucart-side-a and bodart-strength); the passages read do not show what it counts. His about 56,000 is the two corps united, which did not fight together. Which French troops were present followed from Napoleon's orders, the grand-duc de Berg's withdrawal of the dragoons and Bernadotte's reading of his orders, so the claim is inherited. English renderings (ours): 'on the return to Naumburg the marshal had the pass of Kösen occupied by the 25th line infantry regiment, and assembled his generals in order to instruct them in consequence of the preliminary orders already received from Napoleon, which had moved the grand-duc de Berg to march off up the Saale and to take away the dragoon division Sachuc'; 'Marshal Davout also went at once to Marshal Bernadotte, communicated to him the order received and proposed to him to debouch behind him as far as Kösen and to take over the command of the united corps of about 56,000 men'; 'Marshal Bernadotte, however, understood the order differently, and believed he had to march to Dornburg, since Napoleon must have given this order first'; 'Marshal Davout was thus left to his own forces — about 33000 men — but believed, since Napoleon stated that he himself had the whole Prussian army before him, [that he would have to deal] only with a Prussian corps' (p. 365); 'the French division Gudin and the Prussian division Schmettau reach the area of Hassenhausen at about the same time'; '[during the cavalry attack] the battalions of the division Friant had gradually arrived on the battlefield'; 'Marshal Davout led them, as they arrived, against the right wing of the division Gudin, to the right of Hassenhausen'; 'the marshal had the battalions come up at a full run, and with them reinforced little by little the left wing to the left of Hassenhausen and extended it toward the Saale valley'; 'when the division Morand, with ... fresh battalions, together perhaps about ... men, went over to the attack,' (OCR).

claims.value: Side B in the documents Foucart prints: in the 5th Bulletin a corps of 50,000 men of the Prussian left moved to cover the defiles of Naumburg and seize the debouches of Kösen but had already been forestalled by Marshal Davout, and by Foucart's note to it the King's army had left Weimar on the 13th about noon and reached Auerstädt in the evening. Davout reported that the King of Prussia, the Duke of Brunswick, Marshal Möllendorf and more than 60,000 men had disputed the victory with his 3rd corps. A later Bulletin of the Grande Armée composes the army commanded by the King in person of an advanced guard of 10 battalions and 15 squadrons under the Duke of Weimar and 3 divisions — the 1st under the Prince of Orange, 11 battalions and 20 squadrons; the 2nd under General Wartensleben, 11 battalions and 15 squadrons; the 3rd under General Schmettau, 10 battalions and 15 squadrons — with a reserve corps under General Kalkreuth of 2 divisions, each of 10 battalions of Guard or élite regiments, and 20 squadrons; it places the Duke of Weimar's corps still near Eisenach and puts all the Prussian forces at the battle of the 14th, without that corps and the Prince of Württemberg's reserve, at 126,000 men. Counting battalions at 700 men and squadrons at about 120 horses, Foucart estimates the King's army at 44,000 infantry and 10,000 horses, 54,000 men. In the account of Lieutenant-Colonel von der Goltz, which Foucart quotes, the main army, 50,000 strong, had left Weimar on the 13th about noon and reached Auerstädt in the evening, meaning to cross the Unstrut between Freyburg and Laucha on the 14th to join the reserve corps approaching the Saale.
claims.rationale: Read from the page images (pp. 612, 613, 614, 617 and 672), with Foucart's title and the later Bulletin's heading from the OCR (p. 611). The later Bulletin's three divisions and reserve make 52 battalions and 70 squadrons, or 90 if 'each' governs the reserve's squadrons too (our arithmetic), against Bodart's 52 battalions and 80 squadrons (claim bodart-strength). At Foucart's rates the 52 battalions would make 36,400 infantry and the 70 or 90 squadrons 8,400 or 10,800 horses; adding the Duke of Weimar's advanced guard of 10 battalions and 15 squadrons to the 52 battalions and 70 squadrons gives 43,400 infantry and 10,200 horses (all our arithmetic), near his 44,000 and 10,000, although his estimate for Rüchel's corps already includes that advanced guard and the later Bulletin places it near Eisenach; the passages read do not show how he reached his figures. The 126,000 covers Jena (B372a) and Auerstedt together. The 5th Bulletin's, Goltz's and Bodart's 50,000 agree; Davout's more than 60,000 is the opponent's report from the field. Foucart's note to the Bulletin's next sentence, on the two other corps, says that these indications on the Prussian army are only general, and his note on the King's march repeats Goltz's sentence nearly word for word. These are the forces present when the armies met, set by the Prussian march, so the claim is inherited; which of them came into action is claim side-b-engaged. English renderings (ours): the 5th Bulletin, '5th Bulletin of the Grande Armée'; 'Iéna, 15 October 1806' (p. 614); 'a corps of 50,000 men of the left moved to cover the defiles of Naumburg and seize the debouches of Kösen; but it had already been forestalled by Marshal Davout'; Foucart's notes, '2. The King's army had left Weimar on the 13th about noon and had reached Auerstädt in the evening'; '3. These indications on the Prussian army are only general indications' (p. 617); Davout's report, 'Battle of Auerstädt'; 'Marshal Davout to the Emperor'; 'at the bivouac of Auerstädt, 14 October 1806' (p. 672); 'the King of Prussia, the Duke of Brunswick and Marshal Möllendorf and more than 60,000 men disputed the victory with your 3rd corps; it remained ours, as did almost all the enemy artillery' (p. 672); Foucart's title, 'situation of the Prussian army', and the later Bulletin's heading, 'Bulletin of the Grande Armée. Berlin, ... November ...' (OCR); 'the army commanded by the King in person was composed of an advanced guard of 10 battalions and 15 squadrons, commanded by the Duke of Weimar, and of 3 divisions'; 'the 1st, commanded by the Prince of Orange, was composed of 11 battalions and 20 squadrons'; 'the 2nd division, commanded by General Wartensleben, was composed of 11 battalions and 15 squadrons'; 'the 3rd, commanded by General Schmettau, was composed of 10 battalions and 15 squadrons'; 'the reserve corps of this army, which General Kalkreuth commanded, was composed of 2 divisions, each of 10 battalions of the regiments of the Guard or of élite, and of 20 squadrons'; 'this whole army was at the battle of the 14th, except the corps of the Duke of Weimar, which was still near Eisenach, and the reserve of the Prince of Württemberg; which brings the Prussian forces that were at the battle to 126,000 men'; Foucart, 'counting the battalions at 700 men and the squadrons at about 120 horses, one may estimate:'; 'the corps of Rüchel at 23,000 men of infantry and 5,000 horses, that is 28,000 men, including the advanced guard of the Duke of Weimar;' (p. 612); 'the King's army at 44,000 men of infantry and 10,000 horses, that is 54,000 men'; 'the strengths given by Lieutenant-Colonel von der Goltz are very nearly the same; he does not count the advanced guard of the Duke of Weimar'; Goltz, '« ...the Prussian army, says this senior officer, after the loss of the bridge of Naumburg, had at last decided to break toward its left in order to keep to its lines of communication'; 'the main army, 50,000 men strong, had left Weimar on the 13th about noon and had reached Auerstädt in the evening; it intended to cross, on the 14th, the Unstrutt between Freyburg and Laucha in order to unite with the reserve corps, which was approaching the Saale' (p. 613).

claims.rationale: Höpfner's reflections (p. 481), his reckoning (p. 366) and the reserve (p. 462), read from the page images, with the army's order from the OCR. His 50,000 equals Bodart's (claim bodart-strength); his 48—49,000 is a reckoning ('mochte'). The reserve's 13 battalions and the 4 Guard battalions make 17 (our arithmetic), against the later Bulletin's 20 for Kalkreuth's reserve (claim foucart-side-b); the passages read do not show whether the 13 leave out battalions already detached, such as the 1st battalion Arnim. These are the forces present when the armies met, set by the Prussian march, so the claim is inherited; how many came into action is claim side-b-engaged. claims.value: Side B's engaged force: in Höpfner the Prussian divisions came into the fight one after another. The division Schmettau met Gudin's at Hassenhausen; the division Wartensleben arrived and attacked with Schmettau's but could not take the village; the division Oranien reinforced both wings but came too late to act as a reserve, finding only remnants of the two other divisions, and had to retreat with them (OCR so far). The reserve of General Kalkreuth, without the 4 Guard battalions and the cavalry, deployed about noon between Gernstädt and Lisdorf, still 13 battalions and 32 guns of fresh troops. Major Jagow led the regiment Zenge toward Lisdorf on his own responsibility but had to take it back when no other troops followed; when the retreat from Hassenhausen became visible Kalkreuth moved the reserve forward to show it to the enemy; and no shot had yet been fired by the division Arnim, or by the troops posted at Sulza, when the King ordered the retreat. Single units went forward: with the King's approval the grenadier battalion Knebel of the division Oranien and the grenadier battalion Gaudi from the head of the reserve were brought toward Gernstädt to go further forward with the grenadier battalion Rheinbaben, and the Königs-Regiment, the only one left of the brigade Plötz, was sent on Rehhausen to take in the right wing; in the retreat the brigade Malschitzky, the left wing of the division Arnim, fought before Eckartsberga, where the regiment Zenge lost very heavily and General Malschitzky was wounded and taken (OCR from 'Major Jagow'). At Sulza, on the Prussian right, the Guard battalions, a battery and some hussar squadrons stood on the height, and the fusilier battalions Kloch, Oswald and Greiffenberg and the Weimar sharpshooters held the Ilm bridge, the Emsen mill, the hollow of the brook and the Sonnenberg; Morand's troops threw the fusilier battalion Greiffenberg off the Sonnenberg, the Guards went down the height but returned to it under fire from the Sonnenberg, and at the general retreat they took in the light troops in square; the reserve's cavalry was fetched, partly squadron by squadron, into the fire (all OCR). Höpfner reckons that nearly half the infantry that stood against Hassenhausen was killed or wounded. His reflections say that through the delayed deployment the units came into the fight singly and never in mass enough to throw the enemy out of Hassenhausen with a vigorous push (OCR), and criticise the splitting of the reserve, the use of 8 battalions to cover the right flank, and the giving up of the battle before the reserves had been used (the last OCR). In the 3rd corps's journal the reserve, the divisions 'Amim' and 'Kukenheim', stood in line between Auerstädt and Gernstädt from the start of the action, and Kalkreuth appeared with what remained of it and presented an imposing front while the divisions of the main body retreated; earlier, in the King's last effort against the French left, the Weimar sharpshooters, Oswald's battalion, the Guard regiments and part of the reserve had come by Sonnendorf onto the heights along the left bank of the Ilm, and as Morand advanced against them the Guard regiments and most of a division of the reserve were crushed (OCR); in the journal's page image part of the Guards of the 1st division of the reserve retreated along the heights of the left bank of the Ilm by Wickerstädt. Davout reported that the Guards on horse and on foot suffered much.
claims.rationale: The targeted follow-up for this entry's most consequential gap (open questions): Höpfner's page images (pp. 462, 472 and 485) and his account of the battle in the OCR (pp. 429-471), with the fight on the Prussian right at Sulza (pp. 469-471) added to the selection for it, compared with the 3rd corps's journal (OCR and p. 682) and Davout's report (p. 672). Höpfner names the units that fought but in the passages read gives no count of the Prussian troops engaged. The reserve's 13 fresh battalions are 25% of Bodart's 52 (our arithmetic). The units Höpfner places at Sulza, the Guard battalions (4 by p. 462), the fusilier battalions Kloch, Oswald and Greiffenberg and the Weimar sharpshooter battalion, make 8 battalions (our arithmetic), the number his reflections say was used to cover the right flank. His reflections give the force that his alternative plan, the reserves marching by Eckartsberga, would have led against Davout's right flank and rear only in the OCR (figure not restated). The accounts differ on how far the reserve and the Guards fought: Höpfner has no shot fired by the division Arnim or the Sulza troops before the retreat was ordered, yet describes the fusiliers' fight at the Sonnenberg, the Guards' descent and the brigade Malschitzky's fight in the retreat; the journal has the Guards, the Weimar sharpshooters, Oswald's battalion and part of the reserve come onto the heights of the Ilm in the King's last effort and the Guards crushed as Morand advanced (OCR), and Davout the Guards suffering much; Höpfner's reserve deployed about noon, where the journal has it in line from the start. Which Prussian troops came into action followed the Prussian command's handling of the battle (claim side-b-command), so the phase is unresolved. English renderings (ours): Höpfner's headings, 'first moment. The heads of both armies meet at Hassenhausen; the French occupy the village'; 'third moment. The division Wartensleben arrives before Hassenhausen, attacks the enemy together with the division Schmettau, but cannot take the village'; 'fourth moment. The French division Morand reaches the battlefield. The Prussian cavalry makes vain efforts against it. The division Oranien reinforces both wings of the troops at Hassenhausen; but comes too late to act as a reserve, and must begin the retreat together with them'; 'fifth moment. The Prussian reserves take in the troops beaten at Hassenhausen and then begin the retreat themselves, by which the battle comes to an end'; as in claim hoepfner-side-a for Gudin and Schmettau; 'neither on the left nor on the right wing of the fighting troops could the fresh battalions of the division Oranien produce the effect of a reserve, since they found only remnants of the divisions Schmettau and Wartensleben, which had kept themselves in the fire only with the utmost effort' (OCR); as in claim hoepfner-side-b for the reserve (p. 462); 'to meet this, and thereby to give the fight still standing at Hassenhausen a more favourable shape and at the same time to open the retreat on Laucha, the aide-de-camp Major Jagow had proposed to General Count Kalkreuth to have at least part of the reserve march off to the left, first to occupy Lisdorf, but then to advance at the foot of the wooded heights'; 'the general had taken no notice of the proposal, and had ridden to the right wing without an answer'; 'when the major had then led the regiment Zenge forward toward Lisdorf on his own responsibility, in the expectation that the other troops would follow, but this had not happened, he had to lead it back into the line and leave the enemy a free hand for further movements'; 'when the retreat from Hassenhausen had further become visible, General Count Kalkreuth had moved the reserve, which at first had stood so that it could not be seen by the enemy, further forward at about ... o'clock, in order to show it to the enemy'; 'no shot had yet been fired by the division Arnim, any more than by the troops posted at Sulza, when the King, who had gone to the height of Eckartsberga to survey the battlefield better and had already given up the hope of throwing the enemy back on Kösen, gave the order to retreat'; '[Prince Heinrich's adjutant had,] with the King's approval, also brought forward toward Gernstädt the grenadier battalion Knebel of the division Oranien, which had been detached with the led horses, and the grenadier battalion Gaudi, which marched at the head of the reserve, in order to lead both battalions further forward together with the grenadier battalion Rheinbaben'; 'at the same time as the grenadiers advanced, the Königs-Regiment, the only one left of the brigade Plötz, had also been sent forward on Rehhausen to take in the right wing'; 'while the left wing, the brigade Malschitzky, remained in its position for the time being'; 'the brigade Malschitzky still had no order to retreat'; 'the regiment lost very heavily,'; 'General Malschitzky was wounded and taken prisoner;'; 'on the height above the small town of Sulza stood, as mentioned, the ... Guard battalions, the ...-pounder battery Yaber [so the OCR] and some squadrons of hussars; the fusilier battalion Kloch covered the right flank toward the Ilm, held the Ilm bridge with a detachment and patrolled beyond it; the fusilier battalion Oswald and the Weimar sharpshooters occupied the Emsen mill and the hollow of the brook, the sharpshooters at the same time the Lindenholz on the slope of the height of Sulza in the rear; the fusilier battalion Greiffenberg occupied the Sonnenberg and the wood on it'; 'Marshal Davout had indeed noticed the position of the Guards above Sulza, and feared that he might be turned from there on his left flank, for on the arrival of the division Morand he had had a battalion of the ... regiment advance along the Saale and the Ilm, and, at the time when the Prussian divisions began the retreat from Hassenhausen, had ordered General Morand to advance with the ... regiment and the division's artillery, leaving Rehhausen to the right, on Sonnendorf and the Sonnenberg, while the rest of the division and the division Gudin would advance against Rehhausen and Tauchwitz and the greater parts of the division Friant in the left flank of the Prussians'; '[so] that the enemy unexpectedly attacked the fusilier battalion in the flank and threw it down from the height, where it still resisted for a long time in the wood, but finally had to draw back to the Guards with the loss of ... dead, ... wounded and ... prisoners'; 'after a lively skirmish at the hollow, in which the fusiliers and sharpshooters kept the upper hand, the enemy extended his line to the left in order to gain a crossing nearer the Ilm, but was accompanied along the brook by the fusiliers etc., while the Guards sent troops in their place toward the hollow in front and, to support them, went down the height with the battalions themselves. As soon, however, as these came under the fire of the Sonnenberg, they returned to their position on the height'; 'when the order for the general retreat arrived, the fusiliers and Jäger drew back step by step to the slope of the height, followed by the skirmishers and fired on without effect by the artillery. The enemy chasseurs tried in vain to break in. So the light troops reached the height, where they were taken in by the Guards, who had formed a square, and continued the retreat on Auerstädt in good order'; 'the cavalry of the reserve had early on obeyed the call: cavalry forward!, but when it was noticed that the march through Auerstädt, past the infantry, was subject to great difficulties, it had, under the personal leadership of General Count Kalkreuth, left the village to the right, broken down a fence, crossed the Ems brook one by one, and soon come level with the division Wartensleben. At the foot of the height beyond Auerstädt the cavalry halted, formed in squadron columns, and was later fetched by various officers, partly squadron by squadron, and led into the fire, so that it achieved no common activity' (OCR); 'of the infantry that had stood against Hassenhausen nearly half was dead or wounded' (p. 472); 'through the delayed deployment the detachments came into the fight singly and never appeared with a sufficient mass to throw the enemy out of Hassenhausen by a vigorous push;' (OCR); 'with an orderly plan of battle, such as was to be expected from the Duke of Brunswick, the reserve would not have been split up, nor 8 battalions used at one point to cover the right flank, where a fusilier battalion and some guns to occupy the crossing over the Emsen hollow and a squadron of hussars to patrol beyond the hollow and the Ilm would have been quite enough;' (p. 485); 'with such a procedure one would have led against the enemy's right flank and rear a force of ... men, to which Marshal Davout had nothing to oppose;'; '...) that the battle was given up before the reserves had been used' (OCR); the journal, 'extract of the journal of operations of the 3rd army corps' (p. 673); 'meanwhile the chasseurs of Weimar, Oswald's battalion, the regiments of the Guards and part of the reserve were arriving by Sonnendorf on the heights that border the left bank of the Ilm, sending ... companies of infantry along the foot of the valley by the river'; 'the King wished by a last effort to break in the left wing'; 'the Marshal perceives this movement of the enemy and has General Morand go there'; 'the regiments of the Prussian Guards are crushed, as is the greater part of the [OCR 'Indivision'] of the Prussian reserve'; 'at half past midday the Prussian army had begun to give way. At one o'clock it was evacuating the heights of Hassenhausen, and its rout would have been complete had General Kalkreuth not appeared with what remained to him of the reserve'; 'this reserve, the divisions Amim and Kukenheim, had remained in line of battle since the beginning of the action between Auerstädt and Gernstädt at the height of Sulza'; 'General Kalkreuth thus presented an imposing front while the ... divisions of the main body of the Prussian army withdrew in disorder, abandoning a great part of their artillery on the heights of Hassenhausen' (OCR); 'part of the Guards of the 1st division of the reserve made their retreat along the heights that border the left bank of the Ilm by Wickerstädt' (p. 682); Davout's report, 'Battle of Auerstädt'; 'Marshal Davout to the Emperor'; 'at the bivouac of Auerstädt, 14 October 1806' (p. 672); 'the King's two brothers were at this battle; the Guards on horse and on foot suffered much' (p. 672).

claims.value: Side A's command: Marshal Davout led the 3rd corps in person. In the 3rd corps's journal he sent his first aide-de-camp, Colonel Burke, forward with a detachment of chasseurs to bring on a skirmish and get certain information on the enemy's position; General Gauthier had orders to receive the charge of the Prussian squadrons with a regiment of his brigade in square, and Davout, seeing his right outflanked, sent General Petit to that regiment's help with another, followed in echelon by a third, and brought guns forward; he, General Gudin and Generals Gauthier and Petit moved from one square to another, and not a battalion was broken although General Blücher returned to the charge again and again. When Friant's division came up he had a battery that hampered its movements carried by a battalion under Colonel Higonet and told Friant not to let himself be outflanked; he sent help to a regiment left alone on the left of Hassenhausen, and when Gudin's division, turned on its left, was about to give way, Morand's division arrived at the run and Davout went with Morand to its head; seeing the King's last effort to break in the French left, he sent Morand against it, and, profiting from the success of both wings, had the centre advance. From the start he had put all his cavalry on his right wing, the only part of his line where it could act effectively (all OCR so far). In Höpfner, as soon as Davout saw Prussian cavalry threatening his right he ordered the brigade Petit, on its arrival, to reinforce the regiment to the right of Hassenhausen, with another regiment and guns to the left of the village and skirmishers in it linking the two; he led Friant's battalions as they arrived against the right of Gudin's division, detached others of them at once to manoeuvre in the Prussian left flank and rear, and brought Morand's battalions up at a full run to reinforce and extend his left; and, fearing to be turned on his left from the Guards' position above Sulza, he sent a battalion along the Saale and the Ilm when Morand arrived and, when the Prussian divisions began to retreat, ordered Morand with a regiment and the division's artillery on Sonnendorf and the Sonnenberg. Höpfner's reflections say that the Prussians' visible inability to take Hassenhausen let Davout act early, under its cover, against their left wing, in whose prolongation lay their line of retreat, and that Morand's arrival let him use most of Friant's division and reach out as far as Lisdorf, having evidently nothing more to fear for his front (all OCR). At the end, by the journal, he directed a division onto the plateaus before Eckartsberga (OCR) and ordered General Petit to attack the last Prussian position with 400 men, and he bivouacked on the field (OCR). Davout's report praises Generals Friant, Gudin and Morand and General Daultanne, and the 5th Bulletin says he showed distinguished bravery and firmness of character and was seconded by Gudin, Friant, Morand and Daultanne, his chief of staff.
claims.rationale: Read from the page images (pp. 614, 619, 672, 673 and 682) and the OCR as marked. Davout's use of each division as it arrived, the squares, the flank movements of Friant's and Morand's divisions, the advance of the centre and the final attack were his own decisions on the field, so the claim is tagged commander_created. The journal reproduces General Gudin's report, as Foucart notes (claim davout-decision); the cavalry's place on the right is in Foucart's note to the journal (OCR, p. 683). claims.value: Side B's command: the Duke of Brunswick commanded the main army, with the King present. On the evening before the battle the Duke, very weak and exhausted, thought not remotely of a battle between Auerstädt and Kösen and still believed he had to deal only with a detached corps of about 6000 French at Naumburg; the next day's movement was arranged with Field Marshal Möllendorf, Generals Kalkreuth, Schmettau, Wartensleben, Zastrow and Phull and Colonels Scharnhorst and Kleist present, no one from the division Oranien being there and General Blücher not yet arrived. In the morning the march set off in the fog; Möllendorf had Schmettau's main body follow its advanced guard immediately, and Höpfner thinks the eagerness to get at the enemy and catch the French cavalry beyond the defile was the main reason that the usual caution was dropped, the enemy and the ground left unreconnoitred and the lifting of the fog not awaited, Möllendorf vying with the youngest and the impulse reaching even the Duke. General Blücher, who found the King at the head of Schmettau's division and asked for instructions, was referred to the Duke and told only that some enemy cavalry regiments were said to have crossed the pass of Kösen and must be thrown back; on meeting French infantry he sent to the Duke asking for more cavalry and more troops to strike a decisive blow. After the first clash the Duke thought it doubtful to march on before the fog lifted, but Möllendorf believed they must march on without loss of time and the King, assuming they had not met considerable forces, agreed. The enemy was thought too strong to attack at once with the division Schmettau alone, so the division Wartensleben was first to come level, and the Duke made Colonel Scharnhorst responsible for everything on the left wing; the Duke sent the division Wartensleben to the right to take the height right of Hassenhausen, believing that if his infantry gained a footing there victory was certain, Möllendorf ordered the regiment Prinz Louis to take the village with the bayonet, and the Duke had called on a grenadier battalion to take the village when he was shot through both eyes; Schmettau was mortally wounded. Then all general arrangements ceased: the King took over the command definitively, but Möllendorf and every leader, aide-de-camp and staff officer gave orders as well, which was especially ruinous to the cavalry, led forward squadron by squadron. The King, displeased that the division Oranien had not come up sooner, ordered its battalions to reinforce the left wing of the fighting troops and then both wings, as the division Wartensleben could not hold much longer right of Hassenhausen. The reserve, first meant to march by Eckartsberga on Laucha, was ordered to follow the division Oranien through Auerstädt; when Captain Tiedemann of the general staff proposed once more to General Arnim, in Kalkreuth's absence, to march by Reisdorf to Eckartsberga and decide the battle by turning the enemy's right, the general would not depart from the order he had received, and Kalkreuth took no notice of Major Jagow's proposal to move part of the reserve on Lisdorf. The King, from the height of Eckartsberga, having given up hope of throwing the enemy back on Kösen, ordered the retreat, first toward Sömmerda and then on Weimar, to unite with Prince Hohenlohe and renew the battle the next day; he countermanded General Blücher's attack with the cavalry and had General Kalkreuth lead the army back (OCR from 'In the morning'). Höpfner's reflections say that on the Prussian side the passage from the march disposition to a plan of battle was wholly lacking: no one knew what to do and the troops went into the fight without knowing what was wanted; with an orderly plan the reserve would not have been split up nor 8 battalions spent covering the right flank, and the reserves would have marched by Eckartsberga to turn Davout's right. They also call it unwise to have let General Blücher attack the infantry his cavalry met in the fog, and say that after the Duke's mortal wound all unity in the arrangements for continuing the battle was lost, every general, staff officer and adjutant commanding on his own, and that the battle was given up before the reserves had been used (OCR from 'They also').
claims.rationale: Höpfner's page images (pp. 364 and 485) and his narrative and reflections from the OCR. The decisions on the field — the march in the fog, the commitment of the divisions one by one, the King's assumption of command, the handling of the reserve and the order to retreat — were the Prussian commanders' own, so the claim is tagged commander_created. Höpfner's reflections also blame the organisation of the army command, which set beside the Duke a council headed by the King himself instead of leaving him the whole responsibility (OCR). The Duke's mortal wound is also in Davout's report and the 5th Bulletin (claim side-b-losses-reported). English renderings (ours): 'at this arrangement Field Marshal Möllendorf, Generals Kalkreuth, Schmettau, Wartensleben, Zastrow and Phull, Colonels Scharnhorst and Kleist and the Duke's aides-de-camp were present'; 'of the division Oranien nobody was present; General Blücher, who had been ordered to headquarters, was also still missing'; 'the Duke thought not remotely of a battle between Auerstädt and Kösen, but spoke at great length about the position to be taken beyond the Unstrut, and still believed he had to deal with a detached corps of only about 6000 French at Naumburg'; 'the Duke was extremely weak; the hardships of the preceding days, the mental exertions and anxieties about the situation of the army, had exhausted his strength' (p. 364); 'the eagerness to get at the enemy, and the hope of capturing or destroying the enemy cavalry that had gone over the defile, was probably the main reason that the caution otherwise observed was lost from view, the reconnaissance of the enemy and of the ground left undone and the lifting of the fog not awaited, but rather everyone pressed forward, in which the old Field Marshal Möllendorf vied with the youngest, and this impulse communicated itself even to the otherwise so deliberate Duke'; 'the advanced guard of the division Schmettau set off, and since, by the general view of things, it was thought that no interval from the advanced guard was needed, Field Marshal Möllendorf, arriving, ordered that General Count Schmettau should follow immediately with the main body of the division'; 'for his own person the general [Blücher] went forward and found the King at the head of the division Schmettau with the regiment Alvensleben'; 'on asking for instructions he was referred to the Duke, and received only the information that some enemy cavalry regiments were said to have crossed the pass of Kösen already, which had to be thrown back'; 'Colonel Scharnhorst, who had made the same discovery [an enemy infantry line close at hand], met the general [Blücher] there, who at once sent his adjutant, Rittmeister Count Goltz, back to the Duke to report to him that he — the general — was outflanking the enemy, and to ask for more cavalry and more troops in general, with which he then meant to strike a decisive blow'; 'the Duke had, as mentioned, thought it doubtful to continue the march before the fog had lifted. Field Marshal Möllendorf, on the other hand, believed they must march on without loss of time, and the King joined the latter opinion, since he assumed that they had not run into considerable enemy forces. The division Schmettau had therefore had to set off again'; 'the enemy was thought too strong to attack at once with the single division, and so one wished first to let the division Wartensleben, which was on the march, come level'; 'the Duke sent him [Scharnhorst] to see what the musket fire meant, and had made him responsible for everything that went on on the left wing'; 'when this division had reached the height of Gernstädt, the Duke sent the order to turn off the road to the right, deploy, and advance through the hollow between Rehhausen and Tauchwitz, in order to take the height to the right of Hassenhausen. The Duke was of the view that if he succeeded in gaining a firm footing on that height with the infantry, he was sure of victory'; 'Field Marshal Möllendorf ordered the regiment Prinz Louis of the division Wartensleben to take the village with the bayonet'; 'the Duke had called on the grenadier battalion Hanstein on the left wing of the division Wartensleben to take the village, when he sank from his horse shot through both eyes'; 'General Count Schmettau was busy leading a regiment forward again on the right wing of his division when he was wounded, but hid his condition until he received a second, mortal wound'; 'now all general arrangements ceased. The King did indeed take over the command definitively, but Field Marshal Möllendorf, every single leader, every aide-de-camp, general staff officer etc.'; '[each] likewise made arrangements, which had an especially ruinous effect on the use of the cavalry, which was led forward and used squadron by squadron by everyone who wished to help here or there, so that all common direction of this arm ceased and, despite its superiority, it could nowhere gain a significant effect'; 'immediately afterwards the King had come, had expressed himself very displeased that the division [Oranien] had not come up sooner, and had ordered the left wing of the fighting troops to be reinforced with all battalions;'; 'while one was still busy deploying, a second order of the King had come: to reinforce both wings of the fighting troops, since the division Wartensleben would not be able to hold much longer to the right of Hassenhausen'; 'the two reserve divisions of General Count Kalkreuth were, according to the first arrangement, to march on Laucha'; 'a peasant from Auerstädt had offered to lead them by Reisdorf, Mallendorf, Eckartsberga and Lisdorf into the old road to Laucha, but the general had first had this way reconnoitred by a column guide, to whom it had not seemed wide enough, and when the fire began at Hassenhausen while the reserves still stood behind Auerstädt, it was thought necessary to bring them up for immediate support, and it was ordered that they should follow the division Oranien and, together with the ... battalion of Blücher hussars and part of the Württemberg hussars, halt as general reserve with Gernstädt before them'; 'when it was further noticed that, with the disorder in Auerstädt, a considerable time would also pass before the infantry of the reserve could pass the village, Captain Tiedemann of the general staff proposed to the division com-'; '-mander General Arnim, in the absence of General Count Kalkreuth, once more to march by Reisdorf to Eckartsberga etc., from where the battle could be decided by turning the enemy's right wing, but the general would not depart from the order he had received,'; as in claim side-b-engaged for Jagow's proposal, Kalkreuth's silence and the retreat order; 'it was the King's intention, under the protection of such a position, to have the retiring troops take the road by Buttstädt to Sömmerda, and to direct the corps of Hohenlohe, Rüchel and Weimar there as well'; 'the King believed, however, that Artern might well already be occupied by the enemy, and since he had no knowledge of the fate of Hohenlohe's and Rüchel's corps, he now decided not to go back on Sömmerda either, but on Weimar, in order to unite with Prince Hohenlohe at the Ettersberg and renew the battle the next day'; 'the general [Blücher] asked the King to allow him to fall upon the enemy with the cavalry; then he meant to play him another considerable trick'; '[so] the King also sent an aide-de-camp to the general with the order to refrain from the attack'; 'an aide-de-camp came back with the order: General Count Kalkreuth was to lead the army back' (OCR); 'on the Prussian side the passage from the march disposition to the plan of battle was wholly lacking'; 'nobody knew what was to be done; the troops went into the fight without knowing what was wanted and what they were to do'; as in claim side-b-engaged for the reserve split up and the 8 battalions; 'one would not have drawn the reserves through Auerstädt behind the other divisions, but would have let them begin, if not from the outset, then at the latest at the same time as the advance of the division Oranien, the march by Eckardsberga already ordered'; 'from Eckardsberga they would have thrown back the enemy's turning movement by Lisdorf, Benndorf, Zeckwar and Spielberg and have turned the right flank of Marshal Davout' (p. 485); '[how]ever, when the cavalry drawn forward ran into enemy infantry masses in the fog, it was not wise to allow General Blücher to attack this infantry'; '...) that after the mortal wounding of the Duke of Brunswick really all unity in the arrangements for continuing the battle was lost, every general, every general staff officer and adjutant commanded on his own account and led troops into the fight'; as in claim side-b-engaged for the battle given up; 'the army command had been organised in a highly inexpedient way, in that a council was set beside the Duke of Brunswick, at whose head the King himself stood, instead of leaving the whole responsibility to the Duke;' (OCR).

claims.value: Marshal Davout's decision: on the 13th, at the time a Prussian patrol threw back a French chasseur patrol, Davout was on the road from Kösen to Hassenhausen with his suite to reconnoitre the ground, and from the height behind Hassenhausen he saw the march of the advanced guard of the division Schmettau and part of the division itself; on his return to Naumburg he had the pass of Kösen occupied by the 25th line infantry regiment and assembled his generals. Napoleon's orders, dated 10 in the evening of the 13th from the heights by Jena, reached him only toward 3 in the morning of the 14th: Napoleon, resolved to attack the Prussian army between Jena and Weimar, called on him to direct himself on Apolda to act in its rear, leaving him the road; in the 5th Bulletin Davout had been ordered to debouch by Naumburg, to defend the defiles of Kösen if the enemy marched on Naumburg or to go to Apolda and take the enemy in the rear if he stayed in his position. Davout proposed that Marshal Bernadotte debouch behind him as far as Kösen and take command of the united corps of about 56,000 men, but Bernadotte understood the order otherwise and believed he must march to Dornburg. Davout had kept his generals at his quarters that night, and when the orders came they left at once to set their troops in motion (OCR). By the 3rd corps's journal there was no other road toward Erfurt by Auerstädt and Apolda, as the Emperor had ordered, so it was important to seize the head of the defile in order to deploy; by the marshal's orders given in the night, because of the distance of the 1st division, the movement was made by the left, and General Gudin with the 3rd division crossed the Saale on the bridge of Kösen at half past 6, Gudin's report having the division leave its position at Neuflemming at 4 in the morning and its head cross the defile at 6. Davout reported that, debouching from Kösen, he found the enemy a quarter of a league away, marching to seize that debouch himself, and that the battle was engaged at once. Höpfner says that at Kösen, as at Jena, everything depended on reaching a point on the plateau of the left bank before the Prussians (OCR).
claims.rationale: Read from the page images (pp. 365, 614, 615, 670, 672 and 673) and the OCR as marked. The march on Apolda was Napoleon's order (claim side-a-objectives) and its route through Kösen followed from it ('there was no other road'), but holding the pass on the 13th, the night orders that sent Gudin's division first, and the push to seize the head of the defile and deploy on the plateau were Davout's own, so the claim is tagged commander_created. That he met the Prussian main army at Hassenhausen was not his choice (claim posture). Foucart's note to the journal's 'orders given in the night' refers to p. 670, where the 3rd corps set off immediately and the 3rd division was crossing the bridge at half past 6; the orders themselves are not in the passages read. Foucart notes that, apart from a few details given in his notes, General Gudin's report is reproduced entire in the journal; the journal's half past 6 and Gudin's 6 for the head of the division are the two documents' times. claims.value: Bodart codes the battle at Auerstädt on 14 October 1806 as a victory of the French under Marshal Davout over the Prussians under the Duke of Brunswick: by his rule the winner stands on the left. Davout reported that the victory remained with his 3rd corps, together with almost all the enemy artillery; in the 5th Bulletin his corps not only held but drove back the bulk of the enemy troops for more than 3 leagues; and in Höpfner the King ordered the retreat, the battle being given up before the reserves had been used, and beyond the brook the dissolution was soon complete (OCR).
claims.rationale: Bodart's heading and entry, read from the page image in the frame transcription, with his rule on p. 46; Davout's report and the Bulletin from the page images (pp. 672, 614 and 619); Höpfner from the OCR. claims.value: Side A's losses as reported: in the 3rd corps's journal the 1st division lost 98 officers and 2,181 men killed or wounded, the 2nd 20 and 900 and the 3rd 134 and 3,500, 252 officers and 6,581 men in all, and with the losses of the cavalry, artillery, engineers and staff about a third of the 3rd corps was put out of action. Davout reported that the Emperor had lost many brave men, among them General Debilly and Colonels Vergès, Higonet, Viala and Nicolas, with several others wounded, that several regiments had lost most of their officers, and that the number of wounded was very considerable. The 5th Bulletin, whose account covers Jena and Auerstedt together, estimates the French loss at 1,000 or 1,100 killed and 3,000 wounded, regrets among the generals only General Debilly, and names among the colonels killed Vergès of the 12th line infantry regiment, Nicolas of the 61st, Viala of the 85th and Higonet of the 108th. Höpfner writes that the enemy himself gave his loss as 270 officers and 7000 men.
claims.rationale: Read from the page images (pp. 683, 684, 672, 673, 614, 619, 620 and 471). The journal's printed totals equal the sums of its rows, 252 officers and 6,581 men, 6,833 killed or wounded in the three divisions (our arithmetic); a third of Foucart's 26,000 present would be about 8,700 (our arithmetic). Höpfner's 270 officers and 7000 men make 7,270 (our arithmetic); the passages read do not name the French return he follows. Bodart's 7,100 with 252 officers (claim bodart-losses) lies between the journal's three divisions and Höpfner's figure. The Bulletin's 1,000 or 1,100 killed and 3,000 wounded, 4,000 or 4,100 for both fields (our arithmetic), are fewer than the journal's 6,833 for the 3rd corps's infantry divisions alone. The Bulletin's dead colonels are not divided by field in the passages read; Vergès, Nicolas, Viala and Higonet are the four Davout names. Foucart's note to the journal's cavalry losses, a table of the losses of the 3rd corps's three chasseur regiments (p. 684, note 1), and the ordonnateur Chambon's letter to Davout on the wounded at Naumburg (p. 684, note 3) were read only in the OCR and are not restated, and the fuller details Davout's report promised were not looked for (open questions). English renderings (ours): the journal, 'extract of the journal of operations of the 3rd army corps' (p. 673); 'officers | men'; 'the 1st division lost, killed and wounded together | 98 | 2,181'; 'the 2nd — — | 20 | 900'; 'the 3rd — — | 134 | 3,500'; '[total] | 252 | 6,581', the dashes being ditto marks (p. 683); 'adding to these the losses of the cavalry, the artillery, the engineers and the staff, about a third of the 3rd corps was put out of action' (p. 684); Davout's report, 'Battle of Auerstädt'; 'Marshal Davout to the Emperor'; 'at the bivouac of Auerstädt, 14 October 1806' (p. 672); 'Your Majesty has lost many brave men, among whom I shall cite General Debilly, Colonels Vergès, Higonet, Viala, Nicolas, and several others wounded'; 'several regiments have lost most of their officers; the number of the wounded is very considerable' (p. 672); 'in the coming days I shall have the honour of sending Your Majesty the details needed to make known to it the brilliant conduct of all its officers and soldiers' (p. 673); the 5th Bulletin, '5th Bulletin of the Grande Armée'; 'Iéna, 15 October 1806' (p. 614); as in claim side-a-command for Davout's corps (p. 619); 'on our side we have to regret, among the generals, only the loss of General Debilly, an excellent soldier'; 'among the colonels killed, Colonels Vergès, of the 12th regiment of line infantry;'; 'Nicolas, of the 61st of the line; Viala, of the 85th; Higonet, of the 108th'; 'our loss is estimated at 1,000 or 1,100 killed and 3,000 wounded' (p. 620); Höpfner, 'the enemy had completely stopped the pursuit, since his troops were very exhausted and had suffered great losses'; 'he himself gave his loss as 270 officers and 7000 men' (p. 471).

claims.value: Side B's losses as reported: in the 3rd corps's journal the enemy lost 115 pieces of cannon, about 15,000 men killed or wounded and 3,000 prisoners, and at the end abandoned 20 pieces of cannon to General Petit. Davout reported that the victory remained with his corps together with almost all the enemy artillery, that the number of prisoners was not very considerable because his little cavalry could not exploit the infantry's successes, that the Duke of Brunswick was gravely wounded in the head and the wound thought mortal, that Prussian generals were wounded, among them Prince August, the King's uncle, and that the Guards on horse and on foot suffered much. The 5th Bulletin's results for Jena and Auerstedt together are 30,000 to 40,000 prisoners, among them more than 20 generals including Lieutenant-General Schmettau, 25 to 30 colours, 300 pieces of cannon and more than 20,000 killed or wounded, with Field Marshal Möllendorf wounded and the Duke of Brunswick killed. Höpfner holds a statement of the Prussian loss at Auerstädt impossible because of the uninterrupted retreat until the army's complete dissolution, and says the men's loss may be inferred from the officers': 1 field marshal, 3 generals, 7 staff officers and 36 other officers, 47 officers in all, were killed or died of wounds — the Duke of Brunswick, Lieutenant-General Count Schmettau and Major-Generals Quitzow and Greiffenberg — and 1 field marshal, 5 generals, 34 staff officers and 181 other officers, 221 in all without the general staff and adjutants, were wounded; 57 guns were lost without the battalion guns, and nearly half the infantry that stood against Hassenhausen was killed or wounded. His narrative calls the loss in prisoners great in the retreat of the left wing by Poppel and very considerable in the retreat by Reisdorf, and his reflections call it very considerable among the Prussians beaten in front; for single units he gives losses for the Irwing dragoons and the fusilier battalion Greiffenberg (OCR from 'His narrative', figures not restated).
claims.rationale: Read from the page images (pp. 673, 683, 682, 672, 614, 619, 620, 471 and 472), with the losses in prisoners and the single units from the OCR. The journal's 3,000 prisoners and 115 cannon equal Bodart's, and its about 15,000 killed or wounded are 5,000 more than Bodart's 10,000 (our arithmetic; claim bodart-losses). Höpfner's 57 guns without the battalion guns are about half the journal's 115 (our arithmetic). Höpfner's officers killed and wounded make 268 (our arithmetic), of whom 10 are field marshals and generals, as in Bodart. The Bulletin's results cover Jena (B372a) and Auerstedt together and the prisoners taken in the pursuit to the day of writing; Davout's 'not very considerable' prisoners are his own field on the day, against Höpfner's loss in prisoners 'great' and 'very considerable' (OCR); the journal counts 3,000. Schmettau is among the prisoners in the Bulletin but among the dead in Höpfner and among the fallen generals in Bodart (claim bodart-commanders), and the Bulletin has the Duke of Brunswick killed where Davout's report of the 14th calls the wound thought mortal and Höpfner lists him among those killed or dead of their wounds. English renderings (ours): the journal, 'extract of the journal of operations of the 3rd army corps' (p. 673); 'the enemy lost 115 pieces of cannon, about 15,000 men killed or wounded and 3,000 prisoners' (p. 683); 'the enemy abandoned this fine and last position with such haste that he left 20 pieces of cannon in the power of General Petit' (p. 682); Davout's report, 'Battle of Auerstädt'; 'Marshal Davout to the Emperor'; 'at the bivouac of Auerstädt, 14 October 1806' (p. 672); as in claims foucart-side-b and foucart-side-a for the victory and the prisoners; 'the Duke of Brunswick was gravely wounded in the head; his wound is regarded as mortal'; 'Prussian generals were wounded. Among these is counted Prince August, the King's uncle'; as in claim side-b-engaged for the Guards (p. 672); the 5th Bulletin, '5th Bulletin of the Grande Armée'; 'Iéna, 15 October 1806' (p. 614); 'the results of the battle are 30,000 to 40,000 prisoners,' (p. 619); 'more arrive every moment; 25 to 30 colours; 300 pieces of cannon; immense magazines of subsistence'; 'among the prisoners are more than 20 generals, several of them lieutenant-generals, among others Lieutenant-General Schmettau'; 'the number of the dead is immense in the Prussian army; it is reckoned that there are more than 20,000 killed or wounded'; 'Field Marshal Möllendorf has been wounded; the Duke of Brunswick has been killed; General Rüchel has been killed; Prince Henry of Prussia, gravely wounded' (p. 620); Höpfner, 'as for the battle at Jena, so also for that at Auerstädt, because of the uninterrupted retreat that followed until complete dissolution, a statement of the loss on the Prussian side is impossible'; 'here too, therefore, the loss of the men may be inferred from the loss of officers'; 'there remained [dead] or died of wounds 1 field marshal, 3 generals, 7 staff officers, 36 other officers, together 47 officers'; 'in artillery 57 guns were lost, without the battalion cannon'; as in claim side-b-engaged for the infantry at Hassenhausen (p. 472); 'but even so the loss in prisoners was great'; 'but the loss in prisoners was nevertheless very considerable'; 'the consequence was that the loss in prisoners on the part of the Prussians beaten in front was very considerable, and the thought of a retreat over the Unstrut was given up. —'; 'the dragoon regiment Irwing had through canister and musket fire a loss of ... officer and ... men in dead, ... officers, ... men and ... horses in wounded' (OCR); claims.value: Auerstädt is a village in the Prussian province of Saxony, 22 km north of Jena (Bodart). In the 3rd corps's journal the ground beyond the Saale is high and offers fine plateaus, cut here and there by brooks, small ravines and some sunken roads and dotted with many villages, crowned to the north by higher knolls covered with clumps of wood; the Saale is not fordable and its left bank is very steep; the great road from Naumburg to Weimar and Erfurt passes through Kösen, where there is a stone bridge over the Saale, and beyond it one must climb a long, steep slope to the plateau of Hassenhausen. Höpfner calls the defile of Kösen an unassailable post, scarcely 1½ Meilen from the division Schmettau's camp before Auerstädt, and says that, with the road as it then was, the slightest infantry or artillery detachment could have made the climb from the Saale to the plateau impossible (the last OCR). A fog so thick that objects could not be made out at pistol range rose half an hour before daybreak (the journal) and cleared gradually (Höpfner; both OCR). Hassenhausen formed the pivot of Davout's position, with no new hold for his corps until behind the Saale if it were lost, and Höpfner judges that taking it would have decided the battle, since the French had very little cavalry and without the village could no longer hold the plain between it and the Saale; the French in it stood covered up to the neck in the hollow roads, in the houses and behind the hedges, and the Prussians came early into the French fire, which the village's gardens covered (OCR). Battalions of the division Friant, detached by Davout on their arrival, manoeuvred in the Prussian left flank and rear on ground where they had nothing to fear from the superior Prussian cavalry (Höpfner), and Davout put his cavalry on his right, the only part of his line where it could act; the Prussian outflanking movement came first against that wing, where the plain was more open and the folds of ground on the way from Poppel toward Spielberg let the columns climb under cover (Foucart's notes; all OCR).
claims.rationale: Bodart's place note, read from the page image in the frame transcription; the journal (p. 673) and Höpfner (p. 364) from the page images; the rest from the OCR. The ground and the fog were there before the battle, so the claim is inherited; Davout's push to seize the head of the defile and deploy on the plateau is claim davout-decision. English renderings (ours): Bodart, '(village in Prussia, province of Saxony, 22 km north of Jena)'; the journal, 'extract of the journal of operations of the 3rd army corps' (p. 673); 'the ground beyond the Saale is high and offers fine plateaus, which are cut here and there by some brooks, by small ravines and some sunken roads, and over which a great number of villages are spread'; 'these plateaus are crowned toward the north by higher knolls covered with clumps of wood'; 'the Saale is not fordable; its left bank is very steep and also covered with some clumps of wood'; 'the great road from Naumburg to Weimar and Erfurt passes through Kösen, where there is a stone bridge over the Saale'; 'after crossing this river one must climb by a steep and long slope onto the plateau of Hassenhausen' (p. 673); Höpfner, 'the division Schmettau had from its camp before Auerstädt to the defile of Kösen scarcely 1½ Meilen, and could therefore very well still reach this unassailable post on the 13th, as the disposition had indeed prescribed, and scarcely could a forced march have been more justified anywhere;' (p. 364); 'at Kösen this was all the more necessary since, with the direction and condition at that time of the road from the Saale to the plateau, the slightest infantry and artillery detachment could have made the climb of the left edge of the valley impossible' (OCR); the journal, 'half an hour before day a fog had risen so thick that it did not allow objects to be made out at pistol range' (OCR); Höpfner, 'the fog had gradually cleared'; 'Hassenhausen thus formed the pivot of the marshal's position, to which the detachments arriving little by little could attach themselves. If Hassenhausen was lost, no new hold was to be found for the corps until behind the Saale'; 'but the fire was wholly ineffective, since the enemy stood covered up to the neck in the hollow roads, in the houses and behind the hedges'; 'for the moment everything came down solely to taking Hassenhausen in order to decide the battle; for it became ever clearer now that the enemy possessed only very little cavalry, and that, if he had lost the village, he could no longer hold on the plain between it and the Saale'; 'the French had indeed also suffered extraordinarily; but the Prussians considerably more, since early on they [had come] into the enemy's [fire], covered by the gardens of Hassenhausen'; as in claim side-a-command for Friant's battalions and their manoeuvre (OCR); Foucart's notes, as in claim side-a-command for the cavalry; 'the outflanking movement of the Prussian army had first taken place against the right wing of the ... corps, the plain being more open on that side and the debouch from Poppel on Spielberg offering folds of ground by which the columns rose under cover' (OCR).

claims.value: Side A: all the 3rd corps's artillery, reserve included, consisted of only 44 pieces of different calibres (the journal); Davout had little cavalry, not enough to profit from the infantry's successes, the grand-duc de Berg having withdrawn the dragoon division Sahuc the day before; and by Davout's later complaint his cavalry general, Viallanes, despite his entreaties left the marshal's quarters, where the generals were to spend the night, without his knowledge and could not be found when the orders came, so that his cavalry, instead of debouching first, debouched three hours later (OCR). About 7 in the evening, with cartridges lacking and the units much weakened, Davout took position, and the cartridges were to be replaced in the night. Side B: the Prussian divisions reached their bivouacs late, in the cold, dark night, and wood, straw and food could not be brought in under proper supervision, which ended in the plundering of the villages nearby; the troops had cooked and drawn bread, the filled bread wagons were left behind on the Duke's order, and the King's gift of brandy reached few of the troops (OCR). Höpfner's reflections on Auerstädt say the troops went into battle the next morning exhausted and dispirited, without straw, wood and food, and his reflections on both battles that in the rich country the army could not bring itself to requisition and let men and horses go hungry (OCR). On the field the battalion guns of the division Wartensleben stuck in part in the hollow it crossed between Rehhausen and Tauchwitz; guns of the battery Riemer, assigned to the grenadier battalion Rheinbaben, which the King personally ordered forward against Poppel as the division Oranien came up, overturned in the road ditch, and those that could follow had only a few rounds with them, the ammunition wagons not having come up; and with several Prussian battalions the ammunition was already shot off when Morand's division attacked (OCR).
claims.rationale: Read from the page images (pp. 673, 683 and 672) and the OCR as marked. The withdrawal of Sahuc's dragoons was the grand-duc de Berg's, Viallanes's delay his own by Davout's account, the late bivouac and the bread wagons left behind the Prussian command's, and the ammunition spent followed from the fighting, so the phase is unresolved. No return of ammunition or supply on hand for either side was found in the passages read. English renderings (ours): the journal, 'extract of the journal of operations of the 3rd army corps' (p. 673); as in claim foucart-side-a for the artillery (p. 683); Davout's report, 'Battle of Auerstädt'; 'Marshal Davout to the Emperor'; 'at the bivouac of Auerstädt, 14 October 1806' (p. 672); as in claim foucart-side-a for the cavalry and Sahuc; 'cartridges lacking, the units being much weakened, I took position toward 7 in the evening'; 'tonight the cartridges will be replaced, the arms put in order, and tomorrow we shall be ready to carry out Your Majesty's orders' (p. 672); Davout's letter, 'Marshal Davout to the major general. Posen, ... November ...' (OCR); as in claim davout-decision for the night at his quarters; 'despite my entreaties, he [Viallanes] went away without my knowledge at ... in the morning'; 'only at ... o'clock could General Viallanes be found, who showed me on this occasion a bad and dangerous spirit and much insolence, because he felt that he was needed'; '[the result was] that his cavalry, instead of debouching first, debouched three hours later, and that I had it only toward ... or ... o'clock' (OCR); Höpfner, 'the troops continued the march with great zeal, but even so the division Schmettau arrived beyond Auerstädt only at about ... o'clock, where it took up a bivouac on the southern slope of the heights close before the village,'; 'and the reserves, which arrived only between ... o'clock and midnight,'; 'the late arrival of the divisions in the cold, deep dark night caused all kinds of disorder and confusion among the troops, quite unacquainted with bivouacking'; 'wood, straw and food could not be brought in under proper supervision, so that a running to and fro, and finally a regular plundering of the neighbouring villages, followed'; 'the troops had cooked and received bread up to and including the ...'; 'the bread wagons, filled with bread up to the ... October, were still left behind on the Duke's order'; 'the King had made the troops a gift of brandy, but instead of its being brought to the camp, it had to be fetched from Weimar shortly before the march off. When the quartermasters arrived, they found only large casks, so that they had to go back again to fetch small vessels or the field flasks for filling. So it came about that very few of the troops profited from the gift'; '...) that on the ... one set out too late, so that the troops reached the bivouacs only in the dark, and went into the battle the next morning exhausted and dispirited, without straw, wood and food'; 'in that, in the rich country in which one found oneself, one could not bring oneself to requisition, and let men and horses go hungry'; 'the battalion guns [of the division Wartensleben] stuck in part in the attempt to go through the hollow;'; 'the King had personally ordered the grenadier battalion Rheinbaben to advance at once against Poppel'; 'the ...-pounder battery Riemer, which was assigned to the battalion, had overturned ... guns in the road ditch; only ... cannon could follow later; but since the ammunition wagons had not come up, they had only ... rounds in the carriage box'; as in claim hoepfner-side-a for Morand's attack; 'then at last the courage of the Prussian troops, abandoned by all the cavalry and able to bring only little artillery into the fight, was broken, all the more since with several battalions the ammunition was already shot off, and no supports would show themselves anywhere to the rear' (OCR).

claims.value: Side A's information: on the 13th Davout, reconnoitring from the height behind Hassenhausen, saw the march of the advanced guard of the division Schmettau and part of the division; Höpfner adds that he saw Prussian troops arrive at Auerstädt that afternoon but had no idea that he would run into the Prussian main army a Meile beyond the defile of Kösen (OCR). Since Napoleon stated that he himself had the whole Prussian army before him, Davout believed he would meet after debouching at Kösen only a Prussian corps meant to secure the army's rear by holding the pass, while the Prussian main army, after its detachments, may still have counted about 48—49,000 men (Höpfner). In the fog Davout sent Colonel Burke forward to take prisoners and get certain information on the enemy; Burke, meeting no vedettes or outposts, came upon the advanced guard under General Blücher, the King in person marching at its head (OCR). Davout reported that the King of Prussia, the Duke of Brunswick and Marshal Möllendorf with more than 60,000 men had disputed the victory, and that the enemy seemed to have withdrawn toward Weimar. At Jena, by Colonel Blein, the Emperor was uneasy all day about the corps of Davout and Bernadotte and feared the former had been forced at Naumburg; now and then cannon was thought to be heard from that side, the day passed without news of it, and, though he saw that he had not faced the whole Prussian army, he believed the King's army was before him; Napoleon received the news of the outcome at Auerstädt only late in the night (Höpfner).
claims.rationale: Read from the page images (pp. 365, 366, 614, 619, 672, 673 and 426) and the OCR as marked. Davout's expectation came from Napoleon's orders and statement and his own reconnaissance of the 13th, and what he learned in the fog from his own patrol, so the phase is unresolved. His more than 60,000 is above every count of the Prussian army in the passages read (claims bodart-strength, foucart-side-b and hoepfner-side-b). claims.value: Side B's information: on the day before the battle a Prussian patrol under Lieutenant Böhmer met a French patrol between Auerstädt and Kösen, threw it back and took a chasseur, who stated that General Davout had taken Naumburg the day before with his division; it seemed certain that chasseur regiments had crossed the defile of Kösen, and reports put infantry with guns at the pass and bridge of Kösen and more infantry at Naumburg, all of Davout's corps, but on the whole the news of the enemy was contradictory, and the troops arrived too late for any proper reconnaissance of the ground and the enemy; in the night no further news of the enemy and no significant outpost reports reached headquarters at Auerstädt, so everything ordered for crossing the Unstrut at Freiburg and Laucha stayed in force (all OCR so far). The Duke still believed he faced a detached corps of only about 6000 French at Naumburg, and the statements of the head forester at Auerstädt did not change his view. In the morning the Duke remarked to Colonel Scharnhorst that it was a very doubtful thing to advance so, not knowing what was before them (OCR); when the Prussians met the enemy in the fog they believed it only a detachment, and Höpfner holds that once it was certain that a considerable enemy corps was arriving the march dispositions should have been dropped. Later the Prussians judged the enemy far stronger than he was, because they had themselves lost heavily and he had husbanded his forces, and saw the divisions of their main body destroyed while the enemy still showed fresh forces and perhaps further reinforcement from Kösen (OCR). By the account of an officer taken prisoner and brought to the King, which Colonel Blein heard, the King, told that Davout's corps was only 25,000 to 26,000 men, called it French bragging and said there were certainly more than 50,000; and he did not yet know that Hohenlohe and Rüchel had been completely defeated at Jena the same day when he appointed Weimar as the general rendezvous.
claims.rationale: Höpfner's page images (pp. 364 and 485) and his narrative and reflections from the OCR, with the journal and Blein's note from the page images (pp. 673 and 682). What the Prussian command knew came from its patrols and prisoners, and what it failed to learn followed from its late arrival and the fog, so the phase is unresolved. The figures of the prisoner's statement and of the reports on Kösen and Naumburg are read only in the OCR (not restated). 'this man states: that General Davout took possession of Naumburg yesterday with his division, ... men strong'; 'on the whole the news of the enemy coming in was contradictory'; 'it seemed certain: that ... regiments of chasseurs had crossed the defile of Kösen and in the'; 'that the pass and the bridge of Kösen were occupied by about ... men of infantry and ... cannon, Naumburg by about ... men of infantry, and that all these troops belonged to the corps of Marshal Davout'; 'but of a proper reconnaissance of the ground and of the enemy there was no question either, with the late arrival of the troops, as in general the patrol service of the cavalry was not pursued with zeal'; 'when during the night to the ... no further news, and no reports of any importance from the outposts about the enemy, had come in at headquarters at Auerstädt, everything that had already been ordered for crossing the Unstrut at Freiburg and Laucha remained in force for the ... as well' (OCR); as in claim side-b-command for the Duke's belief (p. 364); 'the statements of the head forester at Auerstädt changed nothing in his view' (p. 364); 'the Duke remarked to Colonel Scharnhorst, riding beside him: „it is surely a very doubtful thing to advance like this; one does not know what one has before one.”' (OCR); 'when one ran into the enemy in the fog, one believed one had to deal only with an enemy detachment, and it was therefore quite right that one kept to the previous plan and wished to bring into the fight only as many troops as one believed necessary to clear the enemy out of the way'; 'but when one had gained the certainty that one had to deal with a considerable enemy corps, which though not yet fully arrived was already approaching, then it was time to drop the previous march arrangements and to let the battle grow out of the fight that had begun, both with a view to overwhelming a numerous enemy and with a view to the retreat in case of misfortune' (p. 485); 'one estimated the enemy far stronger than he really was, because one had oneself suffered great losses and the enemy had been far more economical with his forces'; 'one saw the three divisions of the main body destroyed, while the enemy evidently still showed fresh forces, and perhaps even received further reinforcement from Kösen' (OCR);
