claims.value: Side A's objectives: Napoleon, resolved to attack the Prussian army between Jena and Weimar, called on Davout to direct himself on Apolda to act in its rear, leaving him the road; if Bernadotte was with him they were to operate together, though Napoleon hoped Bernadotte had taken the position at Dornburg assigned to him, an order Höpfner says Bernadotte had not received. In the 5th Bulletin Davout was to debouch by Naumburg, to defend the defiles of Kösen if the enemy marched on Naumburg, or to go to Apolda and take the enemy in the rear if he stayed in his position. By the 3rd corps's journal Napoleon left Davout free to take the road that suited him provided he took part in the battle (OCR), and the only road toward Erfurt by Auerstädt and Apolda, as the Emperor had ordered, passed by Kösen, so it was important to seize the head of the defile in order to deploy. Foucart notes that had the 3rd corps not found the King's army on its way it would have reached Apolda about noon, having heard the cannonade since the morning (OCR). After the battle, by Davout's orders, General Viallanes pursued on the right to throw the enemy back to the left, toward the Saale and toward Apolda, the point the Emperor had indicated (OCR).
claims.rationale: Read from the page images (pp. 365, 614, 615 and 673) and the OCR as marked. The objective, to reach Apolda in the Prussian rear and take part in the battle, was set by Napoleon's orders, while the way to it and the conduct of the fight at Hassenhausen were Davout's (claim davout-decision), so the phase is unresolved. claims.value: Side B's objectives: by Höpfner's reflections the Duke did not wish to fight but to march off to the left, cross the Unstrut and place himself again directly before the French, the main army marching off while Prince Hohenlohe was to cover the right flank of its march and then follow (OCR). The disposition for the main army's march announced a retrograde movement, to unite with Duke Eugen of Württemberg and to free the army's rear again, for which the division Schmettau was to set off at once and march to Kösen, taking the pass if it was not strongly held (OCR); Höpfner holds that the division could well have reached that unassailable post on the 13th, as the disposition had prescribed, but the march to Auerstädt was thought long enough and the Duke did not think it urgent. His reflections say the course of the battle had been prepared by the arrangements of the 13th, among them that the division was not sent forward to Kösen that afternoon to occupy the pass and so make sure that the next day's march on Freyburg would not be disturbed: with the pass held, he says, the battle of Auerstädt became impossible (OCR from 'among them'). When a prisoner's report on Davout came in, the Duke had the troops of the main army hasten their march and be ready to engage the enemy that same day, the King intending to attack him at once (OCR). For the next day, as arranged late in the evening at Auerstädt, the army was to set off at daybreak in the same order of march, the division Schmettau following the road to Kösen, its cavalry and advanced guard throwing themselves on the enemy cavalry and an infantry brigade taking and occupying the post of Kösen, the division holding the heights of Kösen until the whole army had passed behind it and defiled across the Unstrut, while the two reserve divisions marched by Eckartsberga straight on Laucha (OCR). In Goltz's account the main army meant to cross the Unstrut between Freyburg and Laucha on the 14th to join the reserve corps approaching the Saale. Höpfner's reflections add that the battle was fought not only to win a victory but to open the retreat across the Unstrut toward the Saale and the middle Elbe, which obliged the Prussians to dare the utmost (OCR). After the battle the King, still hoping to join Prince Hohenlohe and General Rüchel, appointed Weimar as the general rendezvous.
claims.rationale: Höpfner's page images (pp. 364 and 481), Goltz (p. 613) and the journal (pp. 673 and 682), with Höpfner's dispositions and the rest of his reflections from the OCR. claims.value: Both sides attacked. Davout reported that, debouching from Kösen, he found the enemy a quarter of a league off, marching to seize that debouch himself, and that the battle was engaged at once. Höpfner calls it, on both sides, a matter of dispositions after a chance encounter ('Rencontre'), both being surprised by running into a considerable opponent; the heads of both armies met at Hassenhausen, which the French occupied, and the division Gudin and the Prussian division Schmettau reached it at about the same time (the last OCR). The Prussians attacked: General Blücher's cavalry attacked the French infantry at Hassenhausen and was repulsed by the squares; the King ordered the division Schmettau to attack, and Schmettau's and Wartensleben's divisions attacked Hassenhausen but could not take it, the Duke having called on a grenadier battalion to take the village when he was shot; Prince Wilhelm's cavalry charged Morand's division, which received it in square (OCR). The French attacked: while Gudin's division held at Hassenhausen, Friant's went on turning the enemy, advancing between Spielberg and Zeckwar against the Prussian left; Davout sent Morand's division against the King's last effort to break the French left, and Morand outflanked the Prussian army and took it in flank; Davout then had the centre advance (OCR); at the end General Petit, ordered to attack the last Prussian position before Eckartsberga with 400 men, climbed the height with the bayonet without returning the fire and took 20 pieces of cannon.
claims.rationale: Coded both_attacked: a meeting engagement, in which the Prussian main attacks on Hassenhausen and the French main attacks by Friant's and Morand's divisions, the advance of the centre and the final attack before Eckartsberga fell on different parts of the field; neither side fought from a position taken up before the meeting, and the French defence of Hassenhausen and the Prussian reserve's stands before Eckartsberga were parts of a battle that both sides fought by attacking. The accounts agree on the code, so they are one claim. The meeting came from marches set by orders, Napoleon's to Davout and the Prussian disposition to take the post of Kösen (claims davout-decision and side-b-objectives), but the attacks were decided on the field by Davout, the Duke and the King, so the posture is tagged commander_created. English renderings (ours): Davout's report, 'Battle of Auerstädt'; 'Marshal Davout to the Emperor'; 'at the bivouac of Auerstädt, 14 October 1806' (p. 672); as in claim davout-decision for the debouch and the battle engaged at once (p. 672); Höpfner, 'it was a matter here, on both sides, of the arrangements after a Rencontre, for both parties were surprised by running into a considerable opponent' (p. 485); as in claim side-b-engaged for the first and third moments, and in claim hoepfner-side-a for Gudin and Schmettau; 'second moment. General Blücher attacks the enemy infantry at Hassenhausen with some cavalry and is repulsed. The enemy division Friant arrives'; 'the unshaken French squares received him coolly'; 'the King gave the division Schmettau the order to attack, which was begun in echelons from the left wing'; as in claim side-b-command for the Duke's wound (OCR); the journal, '[rein]forced by another numerous corps of cavalry, at whose head was Prince Wilhelm of Prussia'; 'the Prince charged the division Morand several times, but all the units, formed in square, received him coolly with cries of Vive l'Empereur!'; 'the division Gudin was defending itself with advantage level with Hassenhausen, while General Friant with the greater part of his division continued to turn the enemy, advanced between Spielberg and Zeckwar, and was already troubling the Prussians' left flank with a well placed and well directed artillery'; as in claim side-a-command for the King's last effort, Morand and the centre; '[Morand] outflanks and takes the Prussian army in flank; at the same time General Friant, placed likewise on the heights to the right of Poppel, was already outflanking the enemy's left wing' (OCR); the journal, 'extract of the journal of operations of the 3rd army corps' (p. 673); as in claim side-a-command for the last division and Petit's orders (OCR and p. 682); 'General Petit received the fire of the Prussian artillery and that of the musketry without replying; his troops climbed the hill with the bayonet forward, while General Grandeau arrived on the right of this hill with the greater part of the 111th, followed by General Friant and his division'; 'the enemy abandoned this fine and last position with such haste that he left 20 pieces of cannon in the power of General Petit' (p. 682).

claims.value: No passage read has either side fight from works. The French held Hassenhausen with infantry in the village and in the hollow roads running out from it and along the edges of the road, standing covered up to the neck in the hollow roads, in the houses and behind the hedges, and the gardens of the village covered their fire; in Höpfner's reflections the Prussians closed around the village and shattered it with artillery but could not take it, which ended their advance (OCR). Neither Davout's report nor the journal names works. Höpfner calls the defile of Kösen an unassailable post without naming works there.
claims.rationale: Code none_named: the places held were a village with its hollow roads, houses, hedges and gardens, and a defile, without named works; by the brief a village held without named works is not fortified, and the passages read describe no walls or entrenchments at Hassenhausen. The accounts agree on the code, so they are one claim, and a none_named code takes the phase unresolved; none_named reports the passages read, not proof that no works existed. English renderings (ours): Höpfner, 'before this attack of the two divisions the enemy threw himself back into Hassenhausen and into the hollow roads running out from the village and the edges of the road, which were now full of infantry'; as in claim auerstedt-ground for the covered fire, the gardens and the pivot; 'now one runs into the occupied village of Hassenhausen and into infantry masses beside it; one closes around the village, smashes it with the artillery, but cannot take it, and with that an end is put to the advance' (OCR); Davout's report, 'Battle of Auerstädt'; 'Marshal Davout to the Emperor'; 'at the bivouac of Auerstädt, 14 October 1806' (p. 672); the journal, 'extract of the journal of operations of the 3rd army corps' (p. 673); Höpfner, as in claim auerstedt-ground for the unassailable post (p. 364).

open_questions: Deferred: in Foucart, General Gudin's report (Naumburg, 17 October) beyond what his notes to the journal quote; the reports of Generals Friant and Morand and the fuller details Davout's report of the 14th promised, not looked for; Foucart's table of the losses of the 3rd corps's three chasseur regiments (p. 684, note 1) and the ordonnateur Chambon's letter to Davout on the wounded at Naumburg (p. 684, note 3), read only in the OCR and not transcribed; the journal from the debouch to the end of the fight (pp. 673-684), read in the OCR, with its hours, regiment numbers and figures not restated except where transcribed; the 5th Bulletin's text on pp. 616 and 618 (OCR); Colonel Blein's account beyond Foucart's notes on pp. 619 and 682; and the remainder of Davout's letter of 10 November (OCR), cited only for the night of 13-14 October and General Viallanes. In Höpfner, his plan of Auerstädt (cited on p. 362), not inspected; his p. 203 return of the French army, read only in the OCR and not selected; the losses of single units, read only in the OCR (the Irwing dragoons, the fusilier battalion Greiffenberg); and the Prussian retreat beyond the selection's end. Bodart's table of officers' losses, not inspected. Figures read only in the OCR are not restated: among them the hours of the day, the strength of Morand's division, the Guard battalions at Sulza and the battery calibres, the regiment numbers in the journal, and the figures of the prisoner's statement and the reports on Kösen and Naumburg on the 13th.

Most consequential gap: how much of side B came into action. Bodart's 50,000 and the other counts are of the army present; Höpfner says the troops went into the fight piecemeal and the battle was given up before the reserves had been used, and the strength engaged decides whether Davout's corps of 26,000 present (Foucart) fought a force nearly twice its size (our arithmetic) or one nearer its own. The targeted follow-up read Höpfner's account of the battle (pp. 429-471) in the OCR, added the fight on the Prussian right at Sulza (pp. 469-471) to the selection, transcribed his pp. 462, 471, 472 and 485 from the page images, and compared the 3rd corps's journal and Davout's report (claim side-b-engaged). Result: the divisions Schmettau, Wartensleben and Oranien fought at Hassenhausen in succession; of Kalkreuth's reserve, 13 battalions and 32 guns of fresh troops stood about noon between Gernstädt and Lisdorf, and by Höpfner the division Arnim had fired no shot when the retreat was ordered, single units having gone forward to take in the retreating troops and the brigade Malschitzky fighting only in the retreat; the Guard battalions and light troops at Sulza, 8 battalions (our arithmetic), fought a flank action with Morand's troops, in which the fusiliers did the fighting and the Guards went down the height only briefly. The journal has the reserve in line from the start, and the Guards, the Weimar sharpshooters, Oswald's battalion and part of the reserve coming onto the heights of the Ilm in the King's last effort and the Guards crushed as Morand advanced (OCR). No source read counts the Prussian troops that came into action, and Höpfner's divisions are named without strengths in the passages read; a count would need the Prussian order of battle with battalion strengths, beyond this pass's ceiling.

Disputes recorded in the claims: side A's strength (Bodart 36 battalions, 27,300 men and 44 guns; Foucart 26 battalions and 26,000 present of 28,874 effective, with 44 pieces; Höpfner about 33000; Blein's captured officer 25,000 to 26,000); side B's strength (Bodart 52 battalions, 80 squadrons, 230 guns and 50,000; the later Bulletin 52 battalions and 70 or 90 squadrons (our arithmetic) and 126,000 for both fields; Foucart's estimate 54,000; Goltz, the 5th Bulletin and Höpfner 50,000; Höpfner's reckoning about 48—49,000; Davout more than 60,000); the engagement of the Prussian reserve and Guards (Höpfner no shot fired by the division Arnim or the Sulza troops before the retreat order, a fusilier fight at the Sonnenberg and a brief descent by the Guards, the reserve deployed about noon; the journal the reserve in line from the start, the Guards and part of the reserve in the King's last effort and the Guards crushed (OCR); Davout the Guards suffering much); the French loss (the journal 252 officers and 6,581 men in three divisions, about a third of the corps with the other arms; Bodart 7,100 with 252 officers; Höpfner's French self-report 270 officers and 7000 men; the 5th Bulletin 1,000 or 1,100 killed and 3,000 wounded for both fields); the Prussian loss (the journal about 15,000 killed or wounded, 3,000 prisoners and 115 cannon; Bodart about 10,000 killed and wounded, about 3,000 prisoners and 115 cannon, with 380 officers and 12 generals; Höpfner 268 officers killed and wounded (our arithmetic) and 57 guns without the battalion guns, the men's loss not to be stated; the 5th Bulletin's results for both fields); the Prussian prisoners (Davout 'not very considerable'; Höpfner 'great' and 'very considerable' (OCR); the journal and Bodart 3,000); the fates of Schmettau (the 5th Bulletin among the prisoners; Höpfner and Bodart dead) and the Duke of Brunswick (the Bulletin killed; Davout's report of the 14th a wound thought mortal; Höpfner among those killed or dead of their wounds); and the hour Gudin's division crossed at Kösen (the journal half past 6; Gudin's report the head of the division at 6).

Families and dependence: Bodart (a compilation; by his note his side B losses come from French sources, and his 3,000 prisoners and 115 cannon equal the 3rd corps's journal; his French 252 officers equal the journal's; his 10 Prussian generals killed and wounded equal Höpfner's; the passages read do not show his source for the French 7,100, the Prussian 10,000 killed and wounded or the strengths); Foucart (the French staff edition of 1887, printing Davout's report of the 14th, the journal of the 3rd corps, which by Foucart's note reproduces General Gudin's report, Davout's letter of 10 November, the 5th Bulletin and a later Bulletin, with notes quoting Colonel Blein and Lieutenant-Colonel von der Goltz, and his own comments and estimate); Höpfner (the Prussian history of 1850, which reports a French self-stated loss without naming the document in the passages read). Davout's report, the journal and Gudin's report all come from the 3rd corps; the 5th Bulletin is Napoleon's own account; Goltz's account is quoted by Foucart, whose note on the King's march repeats it nearly word for word; the passages read do not show whether Goltz shares sources with Höpfner.
